incidents.description: Reuters reported a fire at Novatek’s Ust-Luga fuel export terminal and condensate-processing complex. The company said it suspended some operations, described the cause as “external influence”, and said the technological process at Novatek-Ust-Luga had stopped pending damage assessment. Regional authorities said workers were evacuated and no casualties occurred; Russian agencies reported two storage tanks and a pumping station damaged. Interfax-Ukraine quoted anonymous sources attributing the fire to a Ukrainian security-services operation, while Reuters said it could not confirm a Ukrainian drone attack. No later actual reopening or present operating condition is established here.

Reuters reported that fuel loadings at Novatek’s Ust-Luga terminal resumed on January 24 after the January 21 fire. The loaded products were produced before the fire and held in storage, with gas condensate also loaded; this is a terminal-loading update, not evidence that condensate processing had restarted. The February 14 Reuters report does not specify the underlying source of this January 24 loading statement, so no operator-origin claim is inferred.

Reuters reported on February 14, citing two industry sources, that Novatek resumed gas-condensate processing at its Ust-Luga complex on February 11. The sources said about 18,000 metric tonnes were processed over February 11–12. Their identities and origins were not specified. This supports processing operation as reported in February 2024; it does not state full capacity or current operation. The February 14 article also distinguishes this processing restart from the earlier January 24 fuel loadings of pre-fire stored products.

Interfax reported, citing Leningrad Oblast Governor Alexander Drozdenko, that open burning at the terminal site in Ust-Luga had been extinguished on Aug. 24, 2025 and the owner’s services would begin repair and restoration work. The article references an earlier report that UAV debris had caused a fire at the Novatek terminal in the port of Ust-Luga. The report does not specify the damaged components, casualties or present operation.

The Kyiv Independent reported that Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) confirmed Ukrainian drones struck the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex at the Baltic Sea port early on Sep. 1, 2026. According to HUR, the strike damaged components of an oil-processing unit and other technological equipment and caused a large fire. The article said damage extent was not immediately clear and does not establish the complex’s present operating status.

This records the attributed fire report only; it does not assert damage extent, independent physical confirmation, or current operation. Reuters said two industry sources told it CDU-1 was damaged and that Lukoil restarted a key unit the prior week after it had been shut this month following attack damage. This records attributed event and subsequent historical restart; no current operating status is asserted.

Reuters reported that local authorities said a fire was extinguished at the Volgograd refinery after a drone attack; Governor Andrey Bocharov attributed the fire to a downed UAV and said there were no casualties. In a separate report that day, Reuters cited a Kyiv source saying two Ukrainian attack drones struck the refinery and that an SBU operation hit the primary-processing facility. Reuters also reported that Lukoil later said the plant was working as normal; this is retained as a Russian operator claim, not a verified operational-status assertion. Reuters’ first report uses a file photo caption dated 22 April 2022, predating this event; the later report displays Reuters credit without an identifying caption in the inspected page.

The report remains attributed; no fire, damage extent, media match, or operational status is asserted. Reuters reported on August 29 that oil processing had been halted since August 28 following Ukrainian drone attacks, citing two industry sources. Those sources said the attack damaged both primary units CDU-4 and CDU-5 and some secondary units; Reuters said the refinery is part of Rosneft’s Samara group, alongside distinct Novokuibyshevsk and Syzran refineries. This is source-attributed detail for the same Aug28 event, not a separate incident or a claim about current operations. Reuters reported on August 29, citing two industry sources, that the refinery had resumed refining on August 21 after completing a major overhaul that began July 1. The reported restart predates the August 28 processing halt described above; it does not establish operation after that halt or present-day status.

Reuters reported on March 25 that the Rosneft-owned Kuibyshev refinery near Samara had halted CDU-5, one of two primary units, after a drone attack over the weekend; two industry sources said this removed about half of its capacity. The report attributes to regional Governor Dmitry Azarov, via Interfax, that a Ukrainian drone attack on Saturday morning, March 23, caused a fire engulfing the primary unit. Reuters’s March 29 factbox later reported, citing industry sources, that all production had halted because of attack damage. These are dated reports; no later or current operating status is inferred.

Reuters reported an explosion at the Rosneft-owned Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara on July 28, citing lawmaker Alexander Khinshtein. Reuters attributed to him that there were no injuries or serious damage and that investigators preliminarily believed an explosive device caused the blast. RIA, citing Rosneft, described the location as a non-operational old building and said no equipment was damaged; TASS said the refinery was undergoing planned seasonal maintenance. Cause, damage and operation details remain attributed; Reuters did not assign responsibility for an attack.

Reuters reported that Rosneft’s Kuibyshev refinery in Samara halted processing on June 10, 2026, after a drone attack. This factbox does not identify the underlying source for this assertion. It records the dated report and does not assert present operating status.

incidents.description: Ukrainska Pravda reported the Ryazan oil refinery was struck overnight on 5–6 September 2026, citing the Ukrainian General Staff; a fire was reported following the strike.

Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed a strike on the Ryazan Oil Refinery on the night of 28–29 July 2026; according to the Ukrainian military, the refinery was hit and a fire broke out on its premises. This remains an attributed account, not independent confirmation.

Interfax reported that Ryazan Region governor Pavel Malkov said a fire occurred on the territory of the Ryazan oil refinery during a mass drone attack on the region overnight and in the morning of 15 October 2026. The governor said the material damage was being assessed; this is an attributed report, not independent confirmation. Interfax separately reported warehouse and vehicle damage at another Ryazan enterprise; that event is not included in this refinery incident.
Reuters reported that Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov said a drone attack caused a fire at the Rosneft refinery on March 13, 2024.
Reuters reported that Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said they struck the Ryazan oil refinery on August 2, 2025, causing a fire on its premises.

Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine’s General Staff and a defence-forces source said strikes caused fires at the Ryazan refinery’s production facilities overnight January 23–24; the strike results were still being confirmed.

Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine’s General Staff said troops hit Ryazan refinery facilities again overnight January 25–26; explosions and fire were reported, with results and damage extent still being confirmed.

Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine’s General Staff said DIU drones struck the Ryazan Oil Refinery overnight February 23–24; five explosions and a fire were reported, with the aftermath still being confirmed.

Reuters reported that Ukraine’s drone-forces commander said drones struck the Ryazan refinery overnight May 14–15, and that Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed a strike and a large fire. Ukrainska Pravda also reported claims of a refinery strike and fire. Interfax separately reported a debris-related fire at an unnamed industrial enterprise in Ryazan; it did not identify the refinery, so that account is kept distinct.

Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Ukrainian General Staff said a strike hit the Ryazan oil refinery on the night of October 22–23, causing explosions and a large fire. Reuters later reported the refinery continued processing at reduced volume after a fire-related interruption on October 23.

Reuters reported that Russian officials said drone attacks occurred in several regions in the hours leading to Wednesday morning; Ryazan governor Pavel Malkov said there were no injuries in attacks there. Baza reported that an attack sparked a fire at the Rosneft-owned Ryazan refinery. Reuters said it could not independently verify the Russian reports. The article page displays publication late on April 30 and refers to Wednesday morning, indicating May 1; exact attack and fire times are not stated.
Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing Ukraine’s General Staff, that Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery in Ryazan on November 15, 2025; the reported results were unknown.
Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing Ukraine’s General Staff, that Ukrainian forces struck the Ryazan refinery overnight on November 20, 2025.

The Associated Press reported on 6 December 2025 that Ukraine’s General Staff said Ukrainian forces had struck the Ryazan oil refinery during the preceding overnight drone attacks. AP said it could not independently verify the video shared by Astra; this candidate makes no media-authentication, damage, or operational-status claim.

Ukrainska Pravda and Reuters reported the Ukrainian commander’s claim that the Ryazan refinery was struck on 5 September 2025. Reuters separately quoted the regional governor describing debris at an industrial site without identifying the refinery; the outcome remains attributed.

Reuters reported on April 15, 2024 that the Rosneft-owned Ryazan refinery had put CDU-4 and its main CDU-6 primary oil-refining units back into operation as Russia restored refining capacity idled by drone attacks. The article did not state the actual restart date for either unit, did not claim full refinery capacity had returned, and did not establish the facility’s later or current operating condition. This is a dated operational update, not a new attack.

Reuters reported on March 28, 2024 that three industry sources said Ryazan refinery CDU-4 had resumed operations during that week after the March 13 shutdown, raising total crude intake to 60% of normal (169,000 barrels per day) at the time of the report. The exact restart day is not specified. Reuters said the sources expected CDU-6 to resume by the end of March; that was a forecast, not confirmation of a later restart. Rosneft did not reply. This is a historical operational update in the existing March 13 incident chain, not another attack or a claim about current operation.

Interfax reported that a fire occurred at the Ryazan refinery on March 1, 2022, citing the regional MChS. Its preliminary account described a fire at a refinery unit over about 100 square meters and reported no injuries or evacuation. RNPK later said the fire was localized at the facility. The article does not establish the cause or subsequent/current operation.

incidents.description: The Associated Press reported that a drone hit the Tuapse oil refinery, damaging some equipment but missing oil reservoirs. The report is based on an AP search-indexed passage that was not visible in the current full-page extraction; the AP source text is preserved as a search-index excerpt. Current operation is unknown.

Ukrainska Pravda reported on Jan. 25, 2024, citing its sources in special services, that the Security Service of Ukraine attacked a Rosneft oil facility in Tuapse during the night of Jan. 24–25. The report says the source attributed a conflagration at the plant to the attack and said the primary petroleum-processing unit was damaged. The article uses “oil depot” in its opening and background but describes damage to a primary-processing unit; this report is recorded with the existing Tuapse refinery complex, not its separately tracked marine terminal. The claim remains attributed; current operation is unknown.

Reuters reporting published May 6, 2024, and republished by the Kyiv Independent on May 7, said two industry sources reported Rosneft’s Tuapse refinery had resumed operations after January drone damage; the sources said repairs to primary unit CDU-12 were completed at the end of April and the unit processed 20,000 metric tonnes on May 1. The exact restart date is not stated; this supports processing by May 1, not a claim that the restart began that day. Source origins are unspecified. The article image caption identifies the RN-Tuapsinsky refinery but dates the Bloomberg/Getty image to March 22, 2020, before the reported restart; it is not event imagery. This historical operating update does not establish later or current operation.

Reuters reported that officials in the Krasnodar region said a fire at Russia’s Tuapse oil refinery broke out after a Ukrainian drone attack and had been contained by May 17, 2024. The reported fire and attack remain attributed; this record does not infer damage extent or ongoing facility operation. Reuters reported in its May 21, 2024 factbox, citing an industry source familiar with the plant, that the refinery resumed operations on Sunday, May 19, after the May 17 attack; Reuters also reported that sources said drones damaged an LPG-producing unit. This is a dated historical report and does not establish current operation.

The Kyiv Independent reported that a second wave of drones struck the Tuapse oil refinery overnight on July 22, 2024; it said debris fell on the refinery, causing damage and a fire later extinguished, while noting it could not verify reports. Ukrainska Pravda separately reported that a Defence Intelligence of Ukraine source said military intelligence drones attacked the named refinery during the same night and that a fire followed. Interfax reported that the Krasnodar regional emergency headquarters said drone debris fell on the refinery, damaging infrastructure and causing a fire that was extinguished; no injuries were preliminarily reported. These reports describe one July 22 refinery event, not separate incidents at the marine terminal. Current operation is unknown.

The Kyiv Independent reported that a source in Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) said Ukrainian drones struck the Tuapse oil refinery overnight on Feb. 26, 2025. The source attributed at least 40 explosions, a fire and damage to oil-refining equipment to the attack; the outlet said it could not verify the claims. Damage is retained only as the source-attributed report; current operation is unknown.
The Kyiv Independent reported that Krasnodar Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said drones struck Tuapse oil refinery overnight on March 14, 2025, setting a gasoline storage tank on fire.

The Kyiv Independent reported that Reuters said Tuapse refinery processing halted on Nov. 2, 2025, a day after a drone attack; its Nov. 5 update attributes the report to industry sources and says the refinery suspended operations because of damage to port infrastructure. This is a historical, attributed processing-interruption report; Reuters later reported processing resumed on Nov. 21. Current operation remains unknown.

Reuters reported on November 24, 2025, citing two industry sources and LSEG ship-tracking data, that the Rosneft-controlled Tuapse refinery resumed oil processing on November 21. The first two tankers mentioned in the article loaded gasoil on November 17 and 18 from product refined before the processing halt and stored in tanks; those port loadings are not evidence that refinery processing had resumed on those earlier dates. Rosneft did not reply to requests for comment. This is a dated historical restart report and does not establish later or current operation.

Reuters reported on Jan28 2026, citing market sources, that Tuapse refinery processing halted on Dec31 2025. The sources estimated it would take another month to restore production to normal; that forecast is not an actual reopening or present-status claim.

Reuters reported on May13, citing two industry sources, that the Tuapse refinery halted operations following a Ukrainian drone attack on April16. The report does not give an actual restart date or establish current operating status.

The Insider reported that the Tuapse refinery was still burning after an overnight drone attack, citing local authorities; it distinguished the refinery from a separate marine-terminal fire. Kyiv Post separately reported an ASTRA identification of a refinery fire and noted that the governor did not confirm refinery damage.

Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine’s General Staff said forces struck the Tuapse refinery overnight on April 19–20, with a fire reported at the facility. This is an attributed account; damage extent and operating effect are not asserted.
The Kyiv Independent reported that Tuapse oil refinery was most recently struck on April 28, 2026, with a multi-day fire ongoing; the outlet said it could not verify its claims at publication.

Reuters reported in its June 26, 2026 factbox that Ukraine’s military General Staff said Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery in the Black Sea port of Tuapse on May 27. The factbox does not identify the source behind the General Staff statement, report damage or operational effects for this May 27 event, or establish current operation.

The Moscow Times Russian Service reported that a fire occurred on the territory of Tuapse Refinery on the night of Oct. 6, 2025, after unmanned aerial vehicle debris fell. It attributed the account to Krasnodar Krai operational headquarters, which said two people were injured. The report does not establish further refinery damage or current operation.

Kyiv Independent reported that Ukrainian forces struck the Kinef oil refinery in Kirishi overnight on March 26, 2026, citing confirmation from Ukraine’s General Staff. Reuters separately reported that two unnamed industry sources said Kirishinefteorgsintez halted processing that Thursday after drone attacks and fires in some plant sections, including two primary and some secondary units; one source could not estimate repair timing. Reuters reported that two industry sources said Kirishi/Kinef was putting back into operation another primary unit damaged by drones in mid-September. This describes a restart process in progress, not a confirmed completed restart; the exact unit, repair completion date and actual achieved throughput were not specified. The same Reuters report said sources expected the plant to work at 70% capacity while CDU-6 was under maintenance; that percentage was a forecast, not a measured operating rate. Surgutneftegas had not immediately replied to Reuters.

The Associated Press reported a September 14 overnight strike and fire at the Kirishi refinery, citing Russian officials and Ukraine’s military. The regional governor said debris from downed drones caused a fire at the facility and that it was put out; AP said the consequences were not immediately verifiable.

Reuters reported that Leningrad region governor Alexander Drozdenko said a tank at the Kirishi refinery was damaged by falling debris during a major Ukrainian drone attack. The governor said one drone was shot down on approach and another destroyed over the enterprise, damaging the external structure of a tank; no one was injured. The extent of refinery damage was not immediately clear, and Surgutneftegaz and Ukraine gave no immediate comment.
